titulo.texto: Monumental Crown of the Dance of the Quetzals

frase_gancho.texto: A crown of colorful rays that spins like a sun.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the dance that spins, we move on to the one that flies. Look for a red costume with golden fringes, scarves crossed over the chest, mirrors, and a conical hat full of flowers and feathers.

guion_corto.texto: This giant crown, more than a meter in diameter, is worn in the Dance of the Quetzals, which is performed in the northern highlands of Puebla, especially among the Nahua and the Totonac. It is built on a frame of cane rods, covered with colored paper, ribbons, mirrors, and feathers. As the dancers bend their bodies and spin, the crown moves like a great colorful sun. Notice the rays that come out from the center, the tassels, and the ribbons that hang down the back. The music is played by a cane flute and a small drum. It is a dance to ask for good harvests and to give thanks to the Sun, and one of the most spectacular in the country.

guion_largo.texto:
Some costumes are worn, and some costumes are carried. The quetzal crown is one of the latter. It measures more than a meter, and to dance with it you need good balance, a strong neck, and a lot of training. It is not a headdress for showing off, but an instrument of dance: it only comes to life when someone moves it.

Its name comes from a bird. The quetzal lives in the cloud forests of southern Mexico and Central America, and its long, iridescent green feathers were worth more than gold. The [feather headdress](mna_s06_penacho_moctezuma) you saw in the Mexica Hall was made with them, and from them comes the name of Quetzalcóatl, the “feathered serpent.” Today the dance headdresses are not necessarily made with quetzal feathers, but with feathers from other birds and with colored paper, yet the name and the idea live on.

Paper and feather are part of a long tradition. In ancient Mexico, the amantecas were the artisans who worked in feather art, and they glued feathers one by one onto fiber bases to create shields, fans, and costumes that seemed made of light. The headdresses of this dance, with their colorful rays, carry on that craft, although with modern materials: tissue paper, ribbons, little mirrors.

The crown represents the Sun. The rays come out from the center, and when the dancers bend and spin, the whole disk moves like a sun that sinks and rises. It is a gesture you already know: the Sun as a central god, from the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol) in the Mexica Hall to the ceremony of the Wixárika. Here it is not painted or carved: it is danced.

Making a crown takes weeks: the cane hoop is assembled, the rays are glued on, the tassels are sewn, and the ribbons are hung. With use it wears out, and every so often it is renewed. Each dancer usually makes or commissions their own.

The music is simple and hypnotic. A cane flute, called pito, and a small drum mark the steps. The dancers move forward in rows, cross paths, spin, and bend, always in rhythm. Seeing them together, with the crowns all spinning at once, is an almost dizzying experience. It is danced at the patron saint festivals of the highlands, such as the one in Cuetzalan, whose name is often explained as “place of quetzals.”

Many people dance out of a promise or a vow, that is, to give thanks for a favor or to fulfill a duty to their community. The crown is prepared months in advance, and sometimes it is inherited. For the dancer, putting it on is an act of commitment. You carry much more than weight: you carry a family history.

In the Oaxaca Hall you will see another feather dance, the [Feather Dance](mna_s17_atuendo_danza_pluma), with another semicircular headdress and another story. It is as if each region had found its own way of wearing the sky on its head. Here, in the highlands of Puebla, that way is a sun of paper and feathers that spins in the mist.

texto.Region: Northern Highlands of Puebla (Cuetzalan del Progreso)
texto.Technique/Material: Reed (cane), tissue paper and metallic paper, satin ribbons, and feathers
texto.Function: Masking paraphernalia and ritual headdress for the Dance of the Quetzals

texto.pregunta: Myth: The headdresses of the Dance of the Quetzals are made only with quetzal feathers.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Today they are made with feathers from several birds and with colored paper, ribbons, and mirrors. The quetzal lives far away, in the southern forests, and the name recalls a very ancient tradition.
